newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: NATO's Solana seeking deal with ex-communists soon.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana seeking deal with ex-communists soon.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Thursday met officials in Uzbekistan to discuss a new partnership with ex-communist states before a controversial NATO summit in Madrid this July.

"We are trying to construct before the month of July what we will call the Atlantic Partnership Council in which we are going to put together the ideas and projects that we have now within the Partnership for Peace programme," Solana told reporters on arrival late on Wednesday in the Uzbek capital Tashkent.

Solana is on a tour of four Central Asian nations in an attempt to convince these ex-Soviet states that NATO's sparring with the Kremlin over its planned eastward enlargement does not threaten stability in their own countries.

"This will be a flexible programme," Solana said. "Every country will be able to take as much as it wants of this project and we hope this will give an impulse to the relations with the countries with which we cooperate now."
Solana, who met Uzbek President Islam Karimov on Thursday, gave no further details on the new partnership plan.
Twenty-seven countries across Europe have signed up for Partnership for Peace, or PFP, which was created in 1994 to fill the security vacuum following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
NATO wants a revamped and reinvigorated PFP to become a permanent feature of Europe's post-Cold War security system.
But PFP members in Central Asia have told Solana this week that they fear Russian anger at NATO expansion could jeopardise regional security.
"Without Russia, there can be no real European security -- we realise this very well," Uzbek Foreign Minister Abdulaziz Kamilov told Reuters in Tashkent.
But "we think that alliance or non-alliance of any state with this or that organisation is its sovereign right," said Kamilov, whose country is the friendliest Central Asian state toward NATO.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites to be the first new entrants to the NATO alliance.
Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev told Solana on Wednesday that he also shared Russian worries over NATO expansion plans.
"We share Russian concerns about NATO enlargement," Akayev said. "Russia is our strategic partner."
But Russian officials on Thursday said they had made progress in negotiations with NATO, opening up the possibility of an agreement with the alliance.
Western diplomats say that Central Asia, physically far from Europe, is also far from NATO's main sphere of interest.
The Central Asian republics themselves remain dependent on Moscow, particularly for energy exports, and are careful to remain on good terms with the Kremlin.
Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, however, plan to hold a joint 10-day regional peacekeeping exercise with NATO in September.
